utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr Registrar, please have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are our interpreters ready? Yes, thank you. Can everyone hear me, my colleagues, the Prosecution, the Defence, General Blaskic, you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLASKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please forgive us for this delay, the Trial Chamber is very much in demand, which is flattering for the judges. We have many motions to deal with and we need time to discuss them, so we take advantage of all the time we have available, so please we wish to apologise for this delay. Ms Paterson, will you please continue, we wish to remind you that we are listening to the testimony of Major Hunter. Thank you, Judge Riad, for reminding me of that. Mr Registrar, can you have -- not the accused, I am sorry, I am a bit distracted, have the witness brought in, please. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is everything in order, Major? Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you had a good rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Ms Paterson, shall we continue with your witness? You have just told us about the first series of incidents relating to 19th May 1993, when fire woke you, I think. Ms Paterson, it is up to you now. MAJOR ROY HUNTER (continued) Examined by MS PATERSON

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr President. Good morning, Major Hunter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to direct your attention this morning to the events of 20th May 1993. On that day, did you have an occasion to attend a meeting at the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after lunch, I took two Warriors and an interpreter and went to the Hotel Vitez in order to meet some of the leaders in the hotel. It was my first meeting with them, in fact it was my last meeting with those people, the one and only occasion I met them. I will just carry on. The people I went to meet were Mr Ante Valenta, Pero Skopljak and Ivan Santic. They identified themselves, Ivan Santic as the mayor of Vitez, Ante Valenta as the deputy President of the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- deputy President of the Croatian Community in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Pero Skopljak identified himself as the -- I will have to check my notes. I have forgotten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Hunter, perhaps if I show you an exhibit that may help to refresh your recollection. Could we have, Registrar, the usher show the witness exhibit number 174?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, yes --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, Major Hunter. Let me just clarify for the court what it is you are looking at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are the business cards the three individuals gave me on arrival at the Hotel Vitez and I made notes on them to translate it into English as they related it to me. Mr Pero Skopljak's card says he is the President of the Croatian Democratic Community in Vitez. On the cards in manuscript, they added their new telephone numbers, because obviously their cards showed their usual telephone numbers before the start of the conflict, so I have the numbers which were either inside Hotel Vitez or in the PTT building, which was next door. These were the two principal headquarters buildings for the HVO in the town of Vitez and for the whole of Central Bosnia, that region. I was met at the entrance to Hotel Vitez, I cannot remember who met me, went through the foyer and just beyond the foyer, in a corridor, was a row of tables on which I noticed there were some radios. These were manned by two or three uniformed soldiers as watch keepers. I was then taken further into the hotel on the ground floor into what I would describe as the manager's office. It was well furnished, there was a large desk, some armchairs, a coffee table. I was in there with an interpreter from our battalion, a Bosnian girl, for about 90 minutes. Over coffee and Slivovic, we just had a long discussion. It was my first chance to meet these characters. We spoke in general about what UNPROFOR was doing in the area, and they gave me their views of the best way forward for solving the conflict in that part of Bosnia. Mr Valenta showed me a small pamphlet he had written a few years earlier, in 1991 or 1992. This was explained to me as a pamphlet which showed the ethnic composition of the various towns and municipalities in Bosnia. There were many pie charts, for example, a town would be shown as 40 per cent Croat, 45 per cent Muslim, 5 per cent Serb, these sorts of charts for each town. His main conclusion at the end was that he had forecast ethnic strife in his pamphlet several years before it had started and that since it was clear that the different communities were unable to live together, it would be necessary for them to live apart. This I interpreted as a requirement to have ethnically pure areas in Bosnia. I was also given a proposal which I made some brief notes of and I took the proposal back to my headquarters so I could brief my commanding officer. I was told the proposal would follow in writing from Colonel Blaskic, but I am not sure whether that letter ever actually arrived. However, the proposal was for the problem of Stari Vitez, which is where some 2,000 Muslims had been contained in the old quarter. They had been held there, unable to move out, since the explosion of the lorry bomb, which I believe was on 16th April, some two weeks before I arrived. The proposal there was that UNPROFOR should go and take the weapons from the ABiH, who were inside Stari Vitez. We would then escort ABiH soldiers out of the old quarter of the town across the lines towards Zenica, and the HVO would then guarantee the safety of any Muslim civilians who remained in Stari Vitez and that the alternative to that proposal, were it not accepted, would be the use of force, which I took to mean the use of force against the military, the ABiH in Stari Vitez. I took notes of that proposal, and briefed my commanding officer when I returned back to the base at Stari Bila and as I said earlier, I do not know whether that letter was actually followed up, whether the letter from Colonel Blaskic actually came to the CO. After some 90 minutes of this conversation, I left the Hotel Vitez. I then had to go around the town, although I was only going about 1,000 metres, I wanted to go to the Franciscan church of Saint George.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Hunter, let me interrupt you at this point to ask you a few additional questions about the meeting at the Hotel Vitez. Do you recall why it was you went to this meeting in the first place? Was it because you wanted to meet these gentlemen, or did they ask to meet with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly. I think it was in order for me to meet personalities for the first time, so I was familiar with some of the leaders in the HVO in Vitez. I should add perhaps that I never went back to the Hotel Vitez, because the system that the commanding officer wanted to use in future, after these very early days, was to have a permanent liaison officer who would liaise with the Hotel Vitez, and that is a man by the name of Captain Lee Whitworth, so he became the CO's personal liaison officer in Vitez, so there was no follow-up meeting, certainly in the Hotel Vitez, for me. I went back one more time a few days later to the PTT building for a second meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Hunter, I just want to remind you, as I did yesterday, that you and I need to slow down and take a pause between our questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that when you entered the Hotel Vitez, you walked through a foyer to another room, and that when you walked through the foyer you saw some radios. Could you describe in some details the radios that you observed at that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With great difficulty. I have really forgotten, I did not pay them a great deal of attention. Because I knew it was the military headquarters, it was no surprise for me that the radios were there. In fact for a long time I was not able remember seeing them at all. It came back to me in April that I had seen them. I paid more attention to the watch keepers, I looked at the people as opposed to the equipment. I believe they were military radios, I think there were two or three, they were what I would expect to have seen in a headquarters of that size, so I am unable to describe the type. They were table-mounted, they were the sort of radios that would also fit in the rear of a vehicle, probably VHF. Certainly if they were British radios of a similar size and were VHF, they would give sufficient coverage over the Lasva Valley, but maybe not as far as the likes of Kiseljak or Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were these radios similar in size and power to radios that you had within the British military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Similar in size, I did not pay sufficient attention to the power, but assuming that the radio technology is of a similar nature then yes, it would be similar to ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that part of the reason you went was to have a discussion with them about a proposal they had to solve the, as you said, problem in Stari Vitez. Do you recall what the situation was in Stari Vitez on that day? You said that the Muslims were still in that area. Can you describe in just a little bit more detail what the situation was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the old quarter in Vitez, centred on the mosque, was perhaps 1,000 metres long and 700 metres wide. The HVO controlled the rest of the town, so this was a small enclave. I understood there were some 2,000 people living in that enclave. The only way in which was still available for use was the main road which ran past the Hotel Vitez, the PTT building, and the police station, which were astride the road. Some 200 metres past those buildings, there was a chicane with some anti-tank mines and then you entered, that was the gateway into Stari Vitez, the chicane was on the HVO side. The other exits from the old quarter had been completely blocked. At the other end of that same road, by the Saint George's church, the road was blocked by a large furniture lorry and an earthen embankment, which was impossible to get by, so there was no movement in and out except for UNPROFOR, we were able to go in and out of Stari Vitez, which we did to take food in to meet with the leaders in Stari Vitez. So that situation remained until I left, actually, until after I left Bosnia in November 1993, in the old town. There were incidents of rifle fire certainly from both sides, mortars, RPG-7, the anti-tank shoulder-launch fire, but there were no major offences. It is very difficult to size an area of buildings of that size, it swallows very many soldiers to seize built-up areas, so there were no major attempts to secure Stari Bila by the HVO -- sorry, Stari Vitez. The ABiH on the high ground around the Lasva Valley --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Hunter, let me just interrupt for a minute. The translators have asked that you slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ABiH to the north of Vitez did make several concerted attempts to break through across the bottom of the valley to relieve Stari Vitez, and they tried that over many months. That was from what we call the mountain road, which was the road from Zenica to Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Hunter, let me just interrupt at this point. When you went to the meeting on 20th May 1993, do you have any idea approximately how many Muslims were still living in the area of Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood there were some 2,000. I went into Stari Vitez maybe 12 times, a lot of times in May and June 1993. I had a lot of dealings with the Hodza in the mosque, the Muslim priest, so he gave me a lot of information about the number of people who had been buried at the back of the mosque, which included many of the victims from Ahmici. He gave me numbers of people who had been arrested and numbers of people who were missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, Major Hunter. Let me ask you a question about the discussion you had with Mr Valenta in which he described for you his writings and his view of the ethnic situation in Central Bosnia. I believe you stated that Mr Valenta was of the opinion that ethnic division was inevitable. Did he explain to you in this conversation how this ethnic division would be achieved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was able to witness on the ground the way it was being achieved, or the way it was occurring, but he did not say that in any words whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, at this time I would like to show Major Hunter an additional exhibit, it is a photograph already in evidence, 80/7. Would you put it on the ELMO please? Okay, Major Hunter, do you recognise any of the people in that photograph and if so, would you explain to the court who you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this man is Ante Valenta. This is the man I had the meeting with in the Hotel Vitez, the author of the pamphlet on ethnic composition. This man I recognise as Dario Kordic (indicates). I saw him attend meetings at our headquarters, although I never met him personally to talk to. This man's face I recognise, but I do not know his name or what position he held. I do not recognise the man in civilian clothes at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just for the record, the man in the photograph with the sunglasses you recognise as Ante Valenta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the man standing behind his right shoulder also with glasses on you recognise as Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding this meeting at the Hotel Vitez, I have one additional question. You said it was your understanding at the end of the discussion that if this plan was agreed to, that the plan would be put in writing in the form of a letter, and the letter would be sent to the British command under the signature of then Colonel Blaskic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those were the notes I made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So even though Colonel Blaskic was not at the meeting with you, you were told that it was his signature that would go on that letter, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Hunter, I would like to continue discussing 20th May, but move to a little bit later in the afternoon. Did you have an occasion then to go on patrol to the area of Donje Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, yes. After leaving the hotel, I had to go all the way around the town, because the road through was closed, as I explained. I had a meeting first of all at Saint George's church with the Franciscan priests and was then returning back towards the base at Stari Bila, but on the way, I took time to drive through Donje Veceriska, with an aim really of just going on to the high ground to a vantage point in order to familiarise myself with the geography.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Hunter, let me just interrupt you at this point. Perhaps it would be helpful if we put an exhibit in front of you that you could refer to as you talk about this. Could we have Exhibit 175 put on the ELMO, please? Okay Major, you may continue and refer to the map when appropriate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This village lies maybe three kilometres to the south west of the town of Vitez. The large industrial things you can see here (indicates) are all part of the Vitez chemical and explosives works, which are obviously a very sensitive location for the HVO. My patrol came up the main road through the village. I noticed in the centre of the village, which I already knew to be a Croat village at this stage, Croat controlled, in the centre of the village, at this junction were a number of civilians and some HVO soldiers in uniform, but not carrying arms. I continued up the road and simply drove to this high point here (indicates). That allowed me to have a very good view of the whole of the Lasva Valley and the town of Vitez. I had already noticed on my way through that there was smoke coming from this area of the village. This is down the side of a hill, it is difficult to tell from this picture, but this factory here is in a very deep valley and these houses were already down a slope. As I drove by, I could not actually see the houses but I could see smoke. It was not an uncommon occurrence to see burning houses at all at that time, but on my way back through the village, I just thought I would go and investigate. As you can see, it is a very sharp corner. The vehicle I was in was a 28 tonne trekked armoured vehicle, so it took me some time to negotiate that corner. It was a neutral corner. It was already clear that my presence down that road was not wanted by either the civilians or the HVO soldiers, but I was in a large vehicle so it was not a particular problem to continue. I stopped the vehicle at the bottom of the hill and dismounted. Here there were four or five houses ablaze, completely ablaze. Their roofs had collapsed. There was no activity, there was no sign of any occupants and I already knew that this village had been cleared of Muslim families five weeks earlier, in the middle of April. I took a few photographs of these burning houses, and at this time one of the HVO soldiers approached me. He had followed down the road on foot, and he wanted me to stop taking pictures, he wanted me to leave the area altogether. He was not aggressive, I had no interpreter with me, but it was quite clear from his gestures that I had no business there and should not be taking pictures of burning houses. I finished what I was doing, left the location and returned to the base. As I say, this was not unusual. In fact, after that, I do not think I took any more photographs of burning houses because it was a daily occurrence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Hunter, before we move on to a couple of other questions, I just want to clarify a couple of points in relation to this photograph. You had an opportunity to look at this photograph before coming to court, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you compare the legend in the corner with the numbers on the diagram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The legend, number 1 is the intersection where there were civilians and HVO soldiers. Number 2 is the burning houses and number 3 is the vantage point I had used to look at the valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said you came to that intersection number 1 on the diagram you saw some HVO; can you describe again how many and how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were only four or five, they were not armed, they were in clean combat uniform. Some of them wore the HVO red and white chequerboard badge, clean shaven, clean boots, had not been involved in anything dirty that day at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then you stated that after going to the vantage point number 3, you returned to the village and went to point number 2 on the map, where you saw the houses burning, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was at that location that you took this photograph, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I took four or five photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we show the Major exhibit number 176, which is another enlargement of this photo? Major Hunter, does this photo show the area where you took this photograph that you have described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does. The arrow is the spot where my vehicle was parked. The photograph I am talking about was taken, I was in this position taking a photograph looking this way (indicates), and you will see that there is an HVO soldier stood in front of my vehicle there, waving me away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we show Major Hunter exhibit number 177, please? Major Hunter, is this the photograph that you took on that occasion of the soldier who was encouraging you to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you just describe for the court in a little bit more detail what this photograph shows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It shows my vehicle in the background, the HVO soldier, who is not armed, he is in the normal combat uniform that soldiers were wearing. The badge, which is very unclear to see on this copy, is the HVO red and white chequerboard badge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an interpreter with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were not able to have a conversation with this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see much point in asking, talking to him, so I finished taking pictures, got in the vehicle and went back to my base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, Major Hunter, you stated earlier that when you went to location 3 on the diagram that you were able to get a vantage looking over much of the valley and back to the village of Donje Veceriska. From there you could see the burning smoke in the village. Can you estimate whether it would have been possible to have seen the burning smoke from this village in the town of Vitez itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you would. The town lies -- I will put this back on. The town centre lies in this direction, to the north east. You would be able to see the smoke, but you would not have seen the flames of those houses, because they were in dead ground. But the smoke would have been clearly visible. But as I say, from any point in the Lasva Valley in those days in May, on a daily basis, you would see houses burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Mr President, I have no further questions, but before we allow cross-examination, let me just move into evidence the exhibits that we have introduced. First of all, exhibit number 172, which is the large aerial photograph. I should explain that as with other such large aerial photographs that have previously been introduced, this photograph was provided to us by the government of Great Britain, pursuant to Rule 70, and I am informed that this photograph was taken on or about 9th November 1994. We would also move into evidence exhibits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms Paterson. 172 is the enlargement. It seems to have been -- it is a montage, what I have here. It seems like a montage.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Mr President, the very large photograph is number 172. Number 173, you are correct, is a montage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, I understand. Any comments from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have previously stated our position, your Honour. Under Rule 70, these photos are supposed to be disclosed to us in advance and they have not been, including this photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. But you are not objecting that they be moved into evidence and you will then discuss them, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is our only comment, your Honour. We have no other comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well then, if there are no further comments, we will number the other exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr President. Just so the record is complete, I am moving into evidence Exhibits 172, 173, 174, which is the three business cards that Major Hunter identified, 175 and 174, the two aerial photos of Donje Veceriska, and number 177, the photograph of the soldier. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. We can now ask Mr Hayman to cross-examine. Cross-examined by MR HAYMAN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr President. Good morning, Major Hunter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: First I would like to ask you a few questions about the events of 19th May 1993 concerning the houses which you described on Exhibit 173, which -- perhaps that can be retrieved, your Honour, and provided to the witness for reference. Would I be correct in stating that as a result of holding the position marked 4 and 4A on Exhibit 173, that the BH-Army controlled the main road at that juncture between Travnik and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they prevented the use of that road by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I say the main road from Travnik to Vitez, in fact is that the road which you can see abutting the line which is 4A on Exhibit 173 after that line turns the corner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is the main road that runs straight through the centre of the picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because they were not able to use that road, did the HVO -- were they forced to use a rough dirt track in order to avoid areas where they would be exposed to fire by the BH-Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the HVO had significantly improved a track about a kilometre and a half to the south of this road, it went behind a very significant hill feature. It had been graded -- it was a very usable road, in fact I used it quite often for my Warriors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is a road they had to construct, basically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. They had made that themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that visible on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not. It is visible on the large photograph on the easel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To go into Vitez on that road, would you ultimately have to go up into some hills and then go back down what is a rougher track?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a bit of military engineering, if you like, to allow HVO movement between Novi Travnik and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were aware in the course of your tour, were you not, that the BH-Army desired to cut the HVO or Croat enclave which was the Vitez-Busovaca enclave, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly after the start of the conflict between those two sides in April, with the clearing of Ahmici and other villages, the BiH organised itself during the month of May and began to close down on the Croatian -- on the HVO enclave, and their main targets were obviously places like the explosives factory, the control of the road through the enclave and the liberation of Stari Vitez from the HVO siege.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All important targets to the BH-Army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, when you arrived in the theatre on 28th April 1993, there was active fighting between the HVO and the BH-Army just north of the village of Santici, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the mountain road across to Zenica and there was fighting in that area through May and into June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the houses marked on Exhibit 173 as point 2, do you have that, Major?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that use of those houses was of concrete military value to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, seizure of that ground and the houses allowed them a better control and a better vantage point across the bridge and across the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a bridge here because there is a river on this map, Exhibit 173, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a small river.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps this could be placed on the ELMO, your Honour, so that the witness could point out, with the usher's assistance perhaps, point out the river so we can see the bridge and exactly what the strategic significance of this location was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The important thing about this is the bridge over the river. This is the only road -- at that time the only road from Split all the way through to Tuzla and it was the road the UN used for all the aid convoys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you first indicate the general flow of the river?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the river flows from here in this direction. It is quite small, it is only about 8 or 9 or 10 metres wide, and about knee deep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it a river such that a bridge is a very useful thing if you are trying to move trucks, cars and the like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. You could cross it on foot with ease and in fact the BiH used to cross it on foot in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point out the bridge that crosses the river?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is just to the left of the white area adjacent to points 2 and 3 on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Try to wait after you ask your question. It complicates things otherwise for the interpreters and for the judges. Thank you for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I know it is very distracting to listen to the presentation otherwise. I will redouble my focus on that. Major, were you ever made aware -- if the map could be moved down slightly on the ELMO, were you ever made aware whether the structure, which is roughly in the shape of an U -- yes, exactly, the one you are locating within the area marked 4 -- behind the line marked 4A on Exhibit 173. Were you ever made aware whether that structure was the command post of the 3rd Battalion of the 325th Brigade of the BH-Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the name of the unit, but I did go into that building. It was occupied by the ABiH. I actually went in as the result of a request from Pero Skopljak on 23rd May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, if you wished to strengthen your position with respect to this bridge and an opposing warring party at 4 and 4A, would you order the houses at point 2 to be occupied by your forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would, yes, but I would not expect them to shoot an old man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would not order them to shoot an old man, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would tell them that these houses are important, go occupy them, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the 60 year old man who was killed on this occasion, do you know how he was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only that he was shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the circumstances were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you were not there to see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, as I said yesterday, I heard the rounds being fired, just the one instance of ammunition being expended from that direction. There was no return fire. I do not know the circumstances, but he was shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a fire in each of these houses on this occasion, within the circle which is marked 2 on Exhibit 173?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least two of them had fires on the ground floor -- are you talking about fire as in conflagration as opposed to bullets?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I am speaking of fire as in flames and smoke.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, two of them were, the large house here that actually stood above the river and had a very good vantage across it and I think possibly this one here, I am not quite sure (indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could point on the ELMO, Major?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. This one here was burning and I think this one. I went as far as here (indicates). I stayed in my vehicle, I did not dismount.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you recall that perhaps two out of the five or six structures within this circle had some sort of fire within them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those fires consume the structures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, as you can see from this photograph taken later, the roof is still intact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The roofs are intact on all of these buildings, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, that would be in the interest of the warring party taking over these buildings not to destroy them if in fact they wanted to use them, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether any soldiers at the scene participated in putting out any fires that may have started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can turn back from the ELMO for the moment, thank you Major. You spoke in your testimony of a later conflict or military action involving this same terrain in September 1993, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we come to that in September, would I be correct in stating that throughout the summer of 1993 the BH-Army continued to hold the positions at 4 and 4A on Exhibit 173?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was very significant ground for the BiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the HVO continued to be denied the use of the road, the bridge and so forth during that time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, until September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall in late August or early September of 1993 the death of four or five Croat children from sniper fire at a location near the UN club, which is a bit above the point marked 3A, that is the letters 3A on Exhibit 173?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour, I believe this is going outside the scope of direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, this is going outside the scope of direct. I am sorry, Mr Hayman, this is completely outside the scope of direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will state for the record, your Honour, the witness described the attack on this location in September 1993 by the HVO. If I am not allowed to establish a rationale and a purpose for that action, then I submit that I would urge the court to rethink that ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ms Paterson, with the assistance of the witness, can you tell us what happened during that attack. Major, could you remind us about what you said, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I described an attack in early September. At this time I was not in Vitez, I was in Germany. I returned on 8th September the day after the attack had been completed. When I returned to the house here, which had actually been very badly damaged by a mortar round, at this time the HVO had succeeded in securing all of the high ground here and the road was now open and there was free traffic, HVO traffic, pedestrians and vehicles, now crossing the bridge. From my colleagues who were in the house who watched it from this location, they described a very successful dismounted attack, with mortar support, which very very quickly indeed secured that feature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You yourself were not there? That is you came after the attack, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the final attack, I was in Santici, unable to proceed along the road to that location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this attack is charged in the indictment under counts 11 and 13, destruction and plunder of property, as an attack on Grbavica in September 1993, that is at page 9 of the second amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I agree. Yes, that is part of the indictment, that is true, but the Prosecutor did not consider that it was important to dwell on that aspect in the testimony at this point. The witness was not there at the time. Ms Paterson, do you wish to add something?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Just, your Honour, that the statement made by the Major on direct was quite limited, simply acknowledging that an attack did occur in September, without going into any significant detail. As he himself has said, he was not present on that occasion. It is our position that this detailed questioning concerning the attack is well beyond the scope of direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I agree with the Prosecution. When you argue your case, Mr Hayman, you can supplement things if you so desire, that is during your part of the trial. Move to another question now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will move on, your Honour. We would ask that Major Hunter regrettably be made available in the Defence case so he can address these issues and illuminate them for the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You will do as you like in accordance with your strategy, Mr Hayman. The presiding judge is not going to be the one to tell you who to bring in and who not to bring in. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am simply seeking the assistance of the court in securing the reappearance of Major Hunter so we do not have to go through a motion for him to appear and so on and so forth. If the court does not wish to address it now, I will not belabour the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, we will not take up that issue right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, Major, to your meeting in the Hotel Vitez on 20th May 1993. You met, as I understand it, with Messrs Santic, Valenta and Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you understand them to be political or civil authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood them to be the political leadership, or representatives of the political leadership, of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say political leadership of the HVO, what would the parallel be in the British military, political or civil authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke of seeing some radios in the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you are not able to identify the models?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at all. I actually made eye contact with the operators rather than look at the equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us that they were not British manufactured radios?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So one could not draw a direct analogy between these radios and a radio in the stock of the British military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only that radio technology is the same all around the world and some of the equipment I was initially trained on was quite old, dating from the 1960s, so I am familiar with what a set of a certain size is capable of doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these look like old sets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would say probably 60s, 70s technology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A proposal was made to you concerning the BH-Army presence in Stari Vitez, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the presence of the BH-Army in Stari Vitez was of military significance to both warring parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, clearly it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you illuminate that answer for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More important was the presence of the Muslim civilian population. I am not sure of the strength of the ABiH in Stari Vitez. It was not large.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this. Would it be a drain on HVO military resources and manpower to have to devote resources to the containment and defence against possible military actions from Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be fairly easy to contain people within that old quarter. What would be much more difficult would be to capture it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself said that during the course of the summer there were attacks in the form of rifle fire, mortar fire, RPG fire, both coming out of Stari Vitez as well as going in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, generally more going in than going out. There were clearly more HVO troops on the outside than there were BiH on the inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those attacks that were coming out of Stari Vitez could directly threaten the Hotel Vitez, the HVO command location, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was not a line of sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could a mortar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An RPG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was line of sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only a mortar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a mortar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came into the theatre, did you read any reports or were you briefed on snipers firing on and indeed hitting HVO negotiators as they were leaving UN Warriors and entering the Hotel Vitez? Does that refresh any recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall anyone being hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that if there was a line of sight sniper fire from BH-Army positions in Stari Vitez to the area of the Hotel Vitez, that would add to the military threat to the HVO from that BH-Army presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was clearly a threat from that presence, a threat both ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you also agree that the BH-Army had as a strategic objective the linking up of other forces such as the Third Corps forces in Zenica with BH-Army forces in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a linking up with the aim of relieving the people besieged in the old quarter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And providing munitions and new ammunition, arms and the like, correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Mr President, we object again that this is beyond the scope of direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I will try to bring some serenity back into this courtroom. We have established a principle which you are familiar with. This comes out of a certain desire for finesse and not for Cartesian geometry. The presiding judge speaking to you is attempting to ensure that the questions of the examination and cross-examination do not fundamentally go beyond the scope of the examination, nor is the presiding judge here in order to stop all possibilities which the judges might have in order to get to the truth. Please, on behalf of my colleagues a while back, I took a decision, because it seemed to me that this was an attack for which the witness had not been present at all. We can allow the Defence to continue and I will be here to stop things if things move too far away from the examination-in-chief. Continue, Mr Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that there was a strategic objective on behalf of the BH-Army to relieve the forces within Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More a humane one, I would have thought, because people in there were quite hungry, obviously, and in fear for their lives. I think the aim would have been to get them out perhaps, or to make the place safer for them to remain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Mr Valenta expressed views which could be described as being in favour of ethnic division, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of Tihomir Blaskic expressing any such views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about whether Colonel Blaskic followed up on this proposal with a letter or not and to your knowledge he did not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not know either way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know either way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do know, correct, that this proposal was followed up on 23rd May 1993 by Mr Skopljak in another contact with UNPROFOR, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a meeting with Skopljak on 23rd May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he state in that meeting, page 4 from your written statement, third full paragraph: "That the BH-Army troops in Stari Vitez should hand over their weapons to UNPROFOR, the Army of BiH would then be allowed to leave Stari Vitez and the HVO would guarantee the safety of the Bosnian Muslims in Stari Vitez."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a repetition of the original proposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that proposal passed on to your commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I briefed the commanding officer and as I said earlier, I do not know whether the letter from Colonel Blaskic was ever received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do know, do you not, that this proposal was relayed to the Army of BiH and was rejected, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let me ask you to turn to your visit to Donje Veceriska later in the day on 20th May 1993. This village was located adjacent to the chemical works or factory, also known as the SPS factory, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was one of the largest explosives and munitions factories in Bosnia, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of tremendous military importance to both warring parties, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely vital.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I could ask the assistance of the Registrar, your Honour, in retrieving Exhibit 164. I do not believe there is any reason this should not be shown to the witness, but I would ask the prosecutors to examine the exhibit before it is given to the witness and to confirm that. I do not believe this was a sealed exhibit, Exhibit 164, involving the testimony of Witness R.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr Hayman. I was speaking with Mr Harmon. Can you repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My question to my learned colleagues across the bar, your Honour, was simply to confirm that there is no reason why this exhibit should not be shown to this witness, Exhibit 164.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The only reason -- there is no problem showing it to the witness per se but it should not be put on the ELMO, because it would identify the witness who testified concerning that exhibit. So as long as it is not put on the ELMO and made public in any way, it is all right for them simply to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You know, I know that you have systems according to which judges are a little bit outside the debate. My practice is somewhat different, so I do not like it too much when you talk about exhibits amongst yourselves. We can have a private session if you like, but to participate in some kind of an agreement in front of the judges, I do not find that quite convenient, and I do not think it is acceptable in any legal system in the world. I do not know what exhibit we are talking about. If we have the agreement of the Prosecution, all the better, but I want to know which exhibit we are talking about, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Of course, Mr President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can cut off the sound, if you prefer, but the judges would like to know which exhibit we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I know these have been given to the court, but I know retrieving them is very burdensome and difficult. Exhibit 164 is an aerial photograph and an accompanying legend that was utilised during the testimony of Witness R, which was yesterday and the day before, which I believe is public testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This witness was in Donje Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, I see. You see, all we needed was a bit of explanation, so I register too that we are not going to have this exhibit on the ELMO, because it could identify the witness. So please continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Major, I was looking at Exhibit 175, which if you do not have it I would ask that you be provided with it. That is the exhibit you have utilised to indicate the points where you saw various things in Donje Veceriska on 20th May 1993. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to find the location of Exhibit 164 that is what it depicts, on Exhibit 175 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr Hayman, please. I should like the judges to have a copy of this exhibit. At least one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I can approach the witness and the court can use my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please continue. I think that we can all talk about this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr President. Are you able to tell us, Major, on Exhibit 164, which houses you saw burning on 20th May 1993, without reference to the house identified as the house of a particular witness. Utilising only the letters, please, and the configuration of circles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to remember. Some of these houses were burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of the houses that are circled on Exhibit 164 at the extreme right-hand edge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them were alight and the others had already been burnt and there was no fire there. I cannot clearly state which of the ones they were. I do have photographs, but not with me, of the buildings which would clarify that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think all of the houses you saw burning on that occasion were houses that are circled on Exhibit 164, or are you not able to make that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Each of these circled houses was either alight or had been burnt already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other houses burning, other than the houses that are circled on the far right-hand extreme of Exhibit 164?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None that I was aware of. The other houses shown as burnt had already been burnt earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have we finished with this exhibit, Mr Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I could just consult with my colleague, your Honour? I think so, but I would like to consult. (Pause). We are concluded with that exhibit, Mr President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then, Mr Registrar, we should like to return this exhibit, because we have it in our record from yesterday's testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Major, during your tour in Central Bosnia, did you encounter any soldiers wearing HV patches, of the Republic of Croatia, in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never saw any. I understood that they were present, but I never saw those badges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they present? What was the basis of your understanding in that regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Briefings which came from the intelligence officer of the British battalion, who received that information from superior headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where in Central Bosnia were you briefed that HV soldiers were present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not given specific locations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever told that HV soldiers were present in the Lasva Valley in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood them to be present in the Lasva Valley, but I never saw the badge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where we might find that information, if you were briefed on some specifics, do you know where we might find that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was never a specific detail, with a place name or that sort of specific information. It was just that it was thought that HV troops were present in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there was never a confirmed sighting by UNPROFOR, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Hunter. No further questions, Mr President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ms Paterson, do you have any further points to clarify in the re-examination? Re-examined by MS PATERSON

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, just very briefly, your Honour. Major Hunter, when you went to the meeting at the Hotel Vitez, you stated that you went to meet with three what you thought to be civilian leaders, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not see the clear distinction between civilian and military in the context of Central Bosnia. Yes, they identified themselves as occupying civilian functions, but a lot of people wore uniform, Mr Ante Valenta himself wore a uniform. I saw it as part of the same organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to the Hotel Vitez for this meeting, was it your understanding that you were going to the military headquarters of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the three buildings, the police station, the PTT building and the Hotel Vitez were three prime control places for the HVO in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you also aware that the Hotel Vitez was where then Colonel Blaskic also had offices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Major Hunter, in reference to the 2,000 Muslims you said that were detained in Stari Vitez, that were the subject of this discussion at the Hotel Vitez, can you give us a rough estimate of how many of those 2,000 people were civilians, women and children, and non-military people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The great majority. Obviously, before the explosion of the lorry bomb, most of the men of fighting age would not have been in the town, they would have been on the frontline engaging with the Bosnian Serb Army. The explosion of that lorry bomb and the sealing off of Stari Vitez left a predominantly old or young population.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no further questions, Mr President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Major Hunter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to your meeting at the Hotel Vitez with Santic, Ante Valenta and Pero Skopljak, you discussed as you mentioned the problem of the ethnic strife, and they came with the conclusion, as you mentioned it, that there should be ethnically pure areas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the light of those, what would be done with the minorities? Where were the minorities supposed to go, were they supposed to be evacuated or killed or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The method of achieving the aim was not explained to me, but the aim was made clear, that the HVO wanted a Croatian Community and only a Croatian Community in Central Bosnia in the Lasva Valley and that any Muslims could go somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that mean that all the minorities would leave or any place where there are Croats should be left to the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The proposal was tied in as well to the Vance-Owen Plan, which was still alive at that time. This created cantons in Bosnia, and these would be under the control of one of the factions, and the canton that was proposed in the Lasva Valley would have been a Croatian canton, and the canton to the north, Zenica, would have been a BiH Muslim canton, so this would tie in with Valenta's policies, that any Muslims in the Lasva Valley ought perhaps to be on the other side of the line in the Muslim canton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the idea was that the Lasva Valley would become Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the bottom line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was quite clear, that this was a Croatian place and Muslims really should not be there --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The proposals you mentioned, one of them that was concerning Stari Vitez, one of them was that UNPROFOR would take weapons from the Muslims and in case they do not give up their weapons, the HVO will use force, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the alternative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was to use force in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to remove the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To remove what, the civilians or the weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not specify. It was the use of force -- the use of force to solve the problem. He did not specify exactly what that meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In another -- when one of your other statements, you said that you were also discussing it I think with Ante Valenta, who did not indicate a solution, but you said that you saw how it was done on the ground. I noted that. How was it done on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the forceful removal or killing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Removal or?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Killing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the Warriors or of the civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of anybody, and then followed by the burning of the houses, barns and the destruction of mosques.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the BiH organised itself in the month of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think the BiH had not expected the attacks of mid April by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was after the attacks then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had to get together sufficient fighting men back into the central Lasva Valley in order to create defensive lines and, as I explained, to try to relieve Stari Vitez. That took quite a long time, there was not a great deal of transport, the movement of armies, soldiers was quite medieval, it was on foot or on horseback. It took time to get men and material in the right place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But all that was after the events of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After Ahmici and Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After Ahmici and the explosion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this did not provoke the events of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was a response to those attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Major, Defence counsel was talking to you about fires burning in certain buildings, and about HVO soldiers being present in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think he asked you about whether any of them participated in putting out the fires, and you said you did not know. Was that your best answer, did you not know, you saw them participating in putting out fires or you saw them not participating in putting out fires?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are the houses opposite the UN base on 19th May. I did not even -- I went across the investigate the buildings. I was aware of some movement amongst the houses, but not a great deal. There were very few soldiers there, maybe just eight, that sort of small group. But they were not -- they did not make themselves come out in the open, they were inside the buildings. I just occasionally could see some fleeting glimpses. Of course, that was a dangerous location, they could be fired on by the BiH, as indeed happened on a daily basis across that bridge. So I cannot clarify. The fires did go out or were put out because the HVO wanted those houses, they became part of their defensive line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you another question. The HVO were in Vitez proper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And ABiH were in Stari Vitez. When you take everything into account, as an experienced military officer, what judgment did you then make as to which side had the military advantage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The BiH in Stari Vitez were at a significant disadvantage. They could only survive on any food that we brought in, although they were able to grow food as well, there were some fields and gardens they could grow food in the summer, but there was no way they could resupply themselves with ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go to a question which Judge Riad asked you. You were talking about the conversation Mr Ante Valenta had with you about ethnic division. Your words, as I took them down, Judge Riad also took them down, were to this effect: "I was able to witness on the ground the way it was being achieved, or the way it was occurring, but he did not say in any words whatsoever." Do I gather from that what you were saying was you understood him to be declaring a policy of ethnic division and an intent to implement that policy, but he did not specify in words the methods by which the policy would be implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my understanding. In fact in my diary that day, I used the word "fascist policy", as a shorthand way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a little question about the military significance which contending military forces may attach to the territory they are defending. Could it be like this, that if you have two opposing military forces, each force may see a distinct military advantage in holding on to its own territory for its own sake. Then you have another situation in which a military force may not see any independent military advantage in holding on to its territory, but would hold on to it merely for some ancillary reason, such as protecting civilians; in other words, if they were not there, that military force would not see any military significance in holding on to that territory. How do you react to this rather convoluted statement of mine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding, the BiH presence was there because they could not get out, you have to accept that there was I think very little movement. There may have been some foot movement across the fields at night, but very low level. My understanding was that they were there to protect the civilian population of Stari Vitez, and that there was no particular advantage from a military point of view of the BiH remaining there, other than the protection of property, a very old mosque from 1590, I think it was, but no military significance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I sum up this phase of your testimony to mean this: that while the BiH was there protecting civilians, they would have seen some incidental military advantage in holding on to some specific position for the purpose of affording that defence to the civilians, but that if the civilians were not there, they would not have seen any military significance in holding on to Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If somehow when the lorry bomb had exploded there had been no civilian population in Stari Vitez but the BiH had been there, I suspect they would not have remained. Probably using UNPROFOR, they would have left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Against all that you have told us, what, in your judgment as a military officer, would have happened to the civilians in Stari Vitez if your military unit had escorted the BiH soldiers out of the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think they would have stayed there very long. I suspect there would have been the use of force to encourage them to leave straight away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard from your intelligence unit that the HV soldiers were present in the Lasva Valley. Did you understand that the HV soldiers were there acting independently or acting in co-operation with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe, this is an opinion, that they would have identified themselves as being of the same group of people, working towards the same end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, drawing on your military experience what is the general position in this scenario, a scenario in which different military units are co-operating with a view to achieving a common objective. Is it the general pattern that to achieve coherence, they would tend to act under a single supreme command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be very dangerous not to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your information and from your observations, was there a supreme military command on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the organisation based in Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic. You may be aware that there was during the summer a Croatian helicopter landing frequently in the quarry about two kilometres south of the British battalion location, so this obviously gives the possibility of communication and bringing in valuable items such as detonators perhaps, which are low in weight but high in value, so there was the possibility of communication right the way through the summer of 1993 between Croatia proper and the HVO enclave in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be right in supposing that the pattern of organisation on the Croatian side was this, that there would have been a political department and the military department, but both acting in co-operation with each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the brain and the arms, if you like, of policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would Colonel Blaskic then have been the military officer tasked with the responsibility of implementing the policies of Mr Valenta and other senior political Croatian leaders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be the logical conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Major, for following these questions. I have only a few clarifications. Concerning the meeting in Hotel Vitez, you spoke about the Vance-Owen Plan. You are not a politician, so you would not like to make any judgments, but you were on the spot. In your opinion, what interest was there in putting into effect by force the provisions of the Vance-Owen Plan, when that plan envisaged that this canton, including the Lasva Valley, was to be Croatian in any event? Was there any particular interest in evacuating by force and violence a territory which, in any event it would appear would have come under Croatian control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the Vance-Owen Plan gave that process a deadline. It was better to achieve this ethnic separation as quickly as possible, so that when the plan came into operation and the cantons were created, the Croat community would have a more secure canton; they would have avoided any problems in the future, perhaps when the area was more peaceful. They were trying to clear the decks, if you like, before the Vance-Owen Plan came into effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a sense it would not be wrong to say that they were preparing against the possible return in the future when this canton really became Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe they were attempting to remove any future problems which a Muslim minority could have caused in the government and the policies of that canton. Possibly there may have been -- I would not have thought there was an imperative perhaps towards that area becoming a part of a greater Croatia, to some sort of union federation with Croatia proper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that same meeting that you attended, was reference made to the customs, the rules and customs of war, respect of civilians, protection of protected persons? Was it referred to by these leaders who were both military and political leaders, or not at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no military leaders present at this meeting. In the words he used, which came to me through an interpreter, I would add, he implied, it was implicit, I think, that the involvement of UNPROFOR would guarantee that this process would be carried out in that manner, but I would say also that I had little faith in that being the case. I saw it as a polite way of explaining the policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you characterise the situation you found in the field during your tour as a situation of war, classical war, or terrorism or -- how would you describe this, as a military man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Lasva Valley it was -- it was not classical war. The position perhaps on the front lines, which had stabilised with the Serb Army, you could call it 19th century-type of warfare, with trench lines and bunkers and some movement, but inside the Lasva Valley, in May and June, no, it was a very unpleasant murderous business. There were purely military operations, of course, and I am also aware that there were very reasonable and decent people involved on both sides, but at the same time, there were some extremely unpleasant personalities and some very unpleasant deeds were committed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it indiscreet to ask you why you took photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the burning houses?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the burning houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at all, no. I had my camera with me throughout the tour, I had only been on the ground at that stage for nine days, it was something that I thought it was worth recording. I did not take many more such pictures afterwards because it was an everyday occurrence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question, and do not answer it if you consider it to be too personal. You have referred to your diary; a personal, intimate diary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I kept a diary from my day of arrival until I left in November. I have it with me, it is just my thoughts, mainly, of what I had witnessed, where I had been, the sort of jobs that we were doing, a lot of personal details as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. I turn to my colleagues, no additional questions? In that case, the Tribunal should like to thank you for coming to testify about your experiences. You can now rejoin your unit. The judges are going to have a 20 minute break and we will resume work at 12.20. The hearing is adjourned. (12.05 pm) (A short break) (12.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume. Have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
